hooks.text: A 100-million-dollar Mars orbiter vanished from a simple math mix-up.
NASA lost a spacecraft at Mars because two teams used different units.
Pounds versus newtons caused a 100-million-dollar Mars disaster.

title: The Mars Mistake That Lost an Orbiter
description: Discover how a unit mismatch between pounds and newtons led to the tragic loss of the Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999.

beats.text: A 100-million-dollar Mars orbiter vanished from a simple math mix-up.
beats.visual: artist's concept of the Mars Climate Orbiter in flight, 1998

beats.text: Most assume it was rocket failure, but the bug was in the software.
beats.visual: Delta II rocket launch carrying Mars Climate Orbiter from Cape Canaveral, 1998
queries: Delta II Mars Climate Orbiter launch

beats.text: Lockheed Martin built the spacecraft to calculate thrusters using pound-force seconds.
beats.visual: Lockheed Martin engineers working on spacecraft assembly, 1998

beats.text: Meanwhile, NASA navigation software expected metric newton-seconds for those exact thrusters.
beats.visual: Jet Propulsion Laboratory mission control room during operations, 1999

beats.text: Since one pound is 4.45 newtons, the computer undercalculated force by nearly 80 percent.
beats.visual: diagram of Hohmann transfer orbit for Mars missions, 1999

beats.text: Those tiny uncorrected errors accumulated over a 9-month journey across space.
beats.visual: Mars atmosphere limb captured by spacecraft in orbit, 1999

beats.text: On September 23, 1999, the probe plunged to a lethal altitude of just 35 miles.
beats.visual: artist's concept of Mars Global Surveyor in orbit, 1999

beats.text: Navigators noticed the drift, but managers ignored them due to missing paperwork.
beats.visual: JPL mission control staff reviewing telemetry data, 1999

beats.text: That bureaucratic failure is why a 100-million-dollar Mars orbiter vanished from a simple math mix-up.
beats.visual: artist's concept of Mars Polar Lander, 1999
